slides.title: DESIGN THINKING  •  LEARNING SERIES
Evidence before assumptions. Learning before scale.
Success looks like a clear user, a meaningful need, a testable promise, and a next experiment.
HCD is not “ask users what to build.” It is a disciplined way to discover the right problem and reduce uncertainty.
REPEAT WITH EVIDENCE
Empathy is not guessing how someone feels; it is staying curious long enough to understand their perspective.
Capture: “I saw…” separately from “I think this means…”. That distinction protects research quality.
Ask about past behavior; silence often gives people space to add the useful detail.
Strong framing links a specific audience + observed need + meaningful insight. Keep the “How might we…” open, not solution-shaped.
NO EARLY PITCHING
A value proposition is a hypothesis until real users respond with evidence—not compliments alone.
UPDATE AFTER EACH TEST
For each concept, name the user benefit, the risky assumption, and the cheapest way to test it.
Choose fidelity to match the question. Don’t build infrastructure to test a message.
Ask: “What would make this fail?” Invite disconfirming evidence.
Facilitator note: map these prompts to the official Forge 231 Ovation Rubric version in use; scoring rules are not specified in this lesson brief.
Test with a small, consented sample. Measure time-to-first-help and repeated questions; never assume a single test proves impact.
Supply chains, infrastructure, and ecosystems have feedback loops. A local fix can create a wider cost—or a multiplier effect.
DELIVERABLE  •  3 evidence-backed insights + 1 testable challenge statement
Design thinking is not a workshop ritual. It is a repeatable habit of learning with people.
